target_customer: Small businesses and marketers who want to answer questions people post on Twitter about their products or industry
problem: Potential customers ask questions publicly on Twitter and most go unanswered. InboxQ searched Twitter for answerable questions matching a business's keywords.
business_model: free tool at launch, monetization not found
product_category: Twitter question finder and engagement tool

founders.name: Joe Fahrner
founders.background_notes: Named on the YC page and TechCrunch (2011-02-17). No bio found.

founders.name: Jason Konrad
founders.background_notes: YC page bio cites infrastructure, databases and data engineering experience. No employers or education listed.

competitors.name: Replyz
competitors.what: Service that also treated Twitter as a Q&A platform, finding and routing questions

technical_complexity.rationale: Needed natural language processing to spot answerable questions in a live Twitter stream; TechCrunch (2011-02) says the earlier product used NLP on Google searches.

defensibility.rationale: Relied on Twitter's open stream and keyword matching, easy for others to replicate and exposed to Twitter policy changes.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Twitter acquired the Q&A service Fluther in December 2010 (TNW, 2010-12-21), showing Twitter's interest in the area. No source shows Twitter copying InboxQ.

market_need_then: CNN Money (2011) said most Twitter questions go unanswered and pitched answering as a way to build reputation. No spend data found.

branding.domain_note: answerly.com now redirects to a GoDaddy for sale page. InboxQ was the product brand from 2011.

rebrands.why: Product refocused on Twitter questions; TechCrunch describes Answerly as the YC company revamping its Q&A product

branding.community_and_virality: Covered by TechCrunch, The Next Web and CNN Money in 2011, plus a Seesmic partnership press release.

brand_strength.rationale: Press coverage in 2011 helped awareness of InboxQ but the YC listing still carries the old name and the name was generic.

pivots.from: Answerly, a Q&A site using natural language processing on Google searches
pivots.to: InboxQ, a Chrome plugin that finds answerable questions on Twitter
pivots.why: TechCrunch (2011-02-17) says the founders shifted focus to Twitter

outcome_analysis: Answerly pivoted from a search based Q&A site to InboxQ in early 2011 and won press from TechCrunch, The Next Web and CNN Money, plus a Seesmic partnership. The YC page now lists it inactive with a team of 11, but no acquisition, shutdown notice or post-mortem was found, so the cause is not public and no failure factor is assigned.
notes: The 20K seed rests on a single database (CB Insights), whose profile mixes in a different Q&A site called Answerly with ANSR tokens, so the investors and the three rounds are unverified. Replyz source date comes from the dated URL and search listing; the page was not opened. Quora, Aardvark and Formspring were Q&A rivals in 2010 but no opened source ties them to Answerly as of the batch. The Freshworks AnsweriQ acquisition is a different company.
